$comment: RBAC-03 field masking — the catalog of client fields a role may hide.
Shaped deliberately like permissions.json, and served the same way (GET
/admin/client-fields), because R-4.5's rule applies identically: the
frontend never invents a key. A mask key with no backend counterpart is not
a cosmetic bug — it is a field an operator believes they hid.
KEYS ARE PATH-QUALIFIED, NEVER FLAT. A bare 'country' is ambiguous between
users.country and the country inside a KYC submission's personal_info JSON.
Masking one while leaking the other is not masking, and a flat key makes
that the default outcome rather than a mistake someone has to make.
'aliases' is what closes that gap in the other direction: a masked key hides
every alias it expands to, so hiding client.phone also removes
personalInfo.phone from GET /admin/kyc/:userId. A test asserts every
identifying/contact client.* field either lists its kyc counterpart here or
carries its own entry — otherwise the KYC screen is a bypass for the whole
feature.
'maskable: false' means the field is structurally required to render a row
at all. Offering it would let an operator configure a screen that cannot
work, and then file a bug about it.
'kyc.user.*' aliases: both KYC responses (the queue row and the detail) also carry the
person under a nested `user` object, so a masked client field has to be removed there too.
'withdrawal.user.*' aliases: the payout desk joins the same person under the same nested
shape, so an operator who ticks 'Email address' once has it hidden there too. Every bypass
this feature has had was a screen that showed a client without going through the client
service. That was a real gap while masking was OPT-IN per response — a surface that
never called the mask leaked whatever the alias named. It is no longer opt-in: a global
response interceptor walks each route's declared DTO and removes what carries
@ClientField, so a new screen is masked by declaring its shape rather than by remembering
to ask. The alias still matters, because it is what tells the catalogue that two names
are the same field; each such surface also keeps its own test.
The desk and its CSV export carry SEPARATE prefixes — 'withdrawal.' nests the person under
`user`, 'withdrawalExport.' flattens it to `userEmail` — because `maskedFields` is a promise
to the screen about THIS response. One shared prefix would have the desk report a flat key
that does not exist on any row it returned, so a UI reading the list would announce a second
hidden field that was never there. The export emits no `maskedFields` (a CSV has nowhere to
put one), so its prefix is invisible and costs nothing. An export must never be a way around
the list it exports, and it no longer is.
'financial.*' / 'financialExport.*': the Financial page (GET /admin/transactions) joins the
same person in both shapes again — nested `user` on the list rows ('financial.'), flattened
`userEmail` in its CSV ('financialExport.') — split for exactly the desk's reason above:
`maskedFields` is a promise about THIS response's rows.
PROFILE FIELDS MOVED HERE (0139). Date of birth, nationality and address used to be
'kyc.personalInfo.*' entries of their own, because they existed only inside a KYC
submission. They are the client's PROFILE now, stored once on `users`, so they are
'client.*' keys like the name and phone, and their KYC spelling is an ALIAS: hiding
'client.dateOfBirth' hides it on the profile, the KYC review and the audit log alike.
Migration 0139 moved every stored mask onto the new keys — and a mask on the address
also took the city and postal code that complete it.

fields.label: Internal record key
fields.reason: Addresses the record inside the system and is shown on no screen — the Portal ID is what identifies a client.

fields.label: Portal ID
fields.reason: Every screen names a client by it — with name and email hidden, it is what still identifies the row.

contact.description: How the client is reached — the most commonly restricted group

profile.description: Account attributes the admin screens filter and sort on

fields.label: Client type
fields.reason: A filter and a column on every client screen; hiding it breaks the list.

fields.label: Account status
fields.reason: Suspend/reactivate decisions are made from it.

fields.label: Verification level
fields.reason: Gates withdrawals; an admin acting without it would act blind.

fields.label: Email verified
fields.reason: Says whether the client can be reached at all. Hiding it would leave a reviewer unable to tell an unconfirmed address from a queued document, which is the distinction this field exists to make.

fields.label: KYC status
fields.reason: The verification decision itself. Approve/reject work is triaged from it, and a masked queue would hide the rows that need doing.

fields.label: Client tags
fields.$why: Segmentation labels ('high risk', 'complaint pending') say more about how the business sees a client than most single fields do, and under tag scoping they also reveal which desks handle them.

fields.label: Introduced by
fields.reason: Records which partner the client came through — a fact about the account, not the person. The partner's name inside it follows the First name and Last name masks, and it needs ib.view to be read at all.
fields.$why: The Referrals page's column (28 Sep 2026). Hiding the whole attribution would make a referred client read as one nobody introduced, which is the false sentence the profile's referrer card was built to stop saying.

kyc.description: Answers to fields a broker added to the KYC form

fields.label: Custom step answers
fields.$comment: Answers to steps a broker configured beyond the four canonical ones, keyed by slug. ONE entry rather than one per field because the fields are invented after this file ships: a role that may not read them loses all of them, which is coarser than kyc.personalInfo and is the guarantee that can actually be kept.

money.description: Where a client is paid, and what they wrote when applying to be a partner

fields.label: Payout destination
fields.reason: A withdrawal is paid to it: whoever approves or settles one has to see where the money goes.
fields.$comment: The bank account, card, wallet address or payment phone a withdrawal is paid to. It was marked 'not a client-owned attribute' on both withdrawal desks, so no role could hide it (D-82). The desks and their CSVs carry it as `destination`.

fields.label: Partner application answers
fields.$comment: The free text a client writes when applying to be an introducing broker: their motivation and website. Free text holds whatever the client chose to tell us (D-82).

fields.label: IP address
fields.$comment: The address a CLIENT acted from, as the audit trail records it. Applied per row in AuditLogStore, not by a DTO mark: the same column holds an administrator's address on every other row (D-82).
